## TL;DR

If a treatment made no difference, the labels "treated" and "control" are arbitrary: each bush would have given the same berries under either label. Shuffling the labels and recomputing the difference, many times, shows the spread of differences that chance alone produces. The p-value is the share of shuffles at least as extreme as the real one, counting the real labelling as one of them. Any statistic works, so you can compare medians when one odd bush drags the mean. Shuffle only what was randomised: whole bushes, not berries, and only within pairs or blocks if the design had them. The answer is exact when the two groups would have the same distribution under the null. When their spreads differ, a test of the raw difference in means can be as misleading as Student's t-test, giving 26.8% false positives in one synthetic case below. In practice: choose the statistic before looking, shuffle units, and use Welch's t as the statistic when spreads differ.
:::

[The t-test](t-test/the_t_test.ipynb) asks whether a difference is large compared with its standard error, and leans on a t distribution to say how large is large. A permutation test builds that reference distribution from the data instead, by asking what the difference would look like if the group labels had been handed out differently. This module covers how it works, what has to be shuffled, and where it fails. All data are synthetic, generated from fixed seeds.

## Shuffle the labels

The recipe has three steps. Pool the measurements from both groups, deal the "treated" and "control" labels out again at random, and recompute the difference; repeat many times. The shuffled differences show what the difference looks like when nothing is going on, and the real difference is judged against them.

The reason this is legitimate is the null hypothesis that the treatment did nothing. Then each bush's yield is a property of the bush, not of its label, and the random draw that decided which bushes were treated is the only thing that made the groups differ. Any other draw was equally likely, so the labels are **exchangeable**: swapping them changes nothing about the probability of what was observed, and every reshuffled difference is one the experiment could just as well have produced. The **p-value** is the share of labellings whose difference is at least as far from zero as the observed one:

$$p = \frac{b + 1}{m + 1}$$

where $m$ is the number of random shuffles, $b$ the number of them with a difference at least as extreme as the observed difference, and the $+1$ in both places counts the observed labelling, which is itself one of the arrangements the null allows. If you instead go through every possible labelling, $p$ is simply the share of them at least as extreme; the observed one is already in the list.

The $+1$ matters: without it a test can report $p = 0$. Phipson and Smyth report that published permutation p-values are often understated by about $1/m$ this way, and argue that the shuffles form an exact discrete null distribution rather than an estimate of a tail probability[^1]. scipy's `permutation_test` adds the one for random shuffles, and the idea goes back to Fisher in 1935[^2].

The widget uses one synthetic trial: mean berry weight per bush (grams) for 8 treated and 8 control bushes. Start at 10 shuffles and note that the running p-value cannot go below $1/11 = 0.091$, whatever the data. Then drag to 5,000 and watch it settle onto the exact value, computed from all $\binom{16}{8} = 12{,}870$ ways to choose which 8 bushes are "treated". Finally switch to medians.

::: {.sim-card}
#### Shuffle the labels

Bars: shuffled differences, orange if at least as far from zero as the observed one (that count is $b$ in $(b + 1)/(m + 1)$). Red dashed lines: the observed difference and its mirror. Lower panel: running p-value (blue) against the exact value (green).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof statChoice = Inputs.radio(["means", "medians", "25% trimmed means"], {value: "means", label: "Compare the groups'"})
viewof nShuffles = Inputs.range([10, 5000], {value: 100, step: 10, label: "Shuffles drawn"})

// Synthetic mean berry weight per bush (g), numpy seed 1935: 8 treated bushes, 8 control.
treated = [1.76, 1.91, 1.84, 1.58, 1.98, 1.97, 1.67, 1.86]
control = [1.54, 1.40, 1.47, 2.12, 1.79, 1.75, 1.36, 1.38]
pooled = treated.concat(control)
nT = treated.length

// One location summary per option; the test statistic is treated minus control.
sorted = xs => [...xs].sort((a, b) => a - b)
avg = xs => xs.reduce((s, v) => s + v, 0) / xs.length
centre = ({
  "means": avg,
  "medians": xs => { const s = sorted(xs), k = s.length >> 1; return s.length % 2 ? s[k] : (s[k - 1] + s[k]) / 2; },
  "25% trimmed means": xs => { const s = sorted(xs), g = Math.floor(0.25 * s.length); return avg(s.slice(g, s.length - g)); }
})

// Difference for one split; idx lists the positions in pooled that get the "treated" label.
splitDiff = (f, idx) => {
  const inT = new Set(idx);
  return f(idx.map(i => pooled[i])) - f(pooled.filter((_, i) => !inT.has(i)));
}

// Seeded generator (mulberry32) so every reader sees the same shuffles.
mulberry32 = a => () => {
  a = (a + 0x6D2B79F5) | 0;
  let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
  t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
  return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
}

// 5000 Fisher–Yates shuffles of the 16 positions; the first 8 of each get the "treated" label.
shuffles = (() => {
  const u = mulberry32(1935), out = [];
  for (let s = 0; s < 5000; s++) {
    const p = [...pooled.keys()];
    for (let i = p.length - 1; i > 0; i--) {
      const j = Math.floor(u() * (i + 1));
      [p[i], p[j]] = [p[j], p[i]];
    }
    out.push(p.slice(0, nT));
  }
  return out;
})()

// Every way to choose which 8 of the 16 bushes are "treated": C(16, 8) = 12,870 splits.
allSplits = (() => {
  const out = [];
  for (let m = 0; m < 1 << pooled.length; m++) {
    const idx = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < pooled.length; i++) if ((m >> i) & 1) idx.push(i);
    if (idx.length === nT) out.push(idx);
  }
  return out;
})()

f = centre[statChoice]
observed = splitDiff(f, [...treated.keys()])
// Two-sided: a shuffle counts if its difference is at least as far from zero as the observed one.
extreme = d => Math.abs(d) >= Math.abs(observed) - 1e-9
exactDiffs = allSplits.map(idx => splitDiff(f, idx))
exactP = exactDiffs.filter(extreme).length / exactDiffs.length
shown = shuffles.slice(0, nShuffles).map(idx => splitDiff(f, idx))
count = shown.filter(extreme).length
// The +1 counts the observed labelling as one of the arrangements.
pRun = (count + 1) / (nShuffles + 1)

// Running p-value after every 10 shuffles.
running = (() => {
  let c = 0;
  const out = [];
  shown.forEach((d, i) => {
    if (extreme(d)) c++;
    if ((i + 1) % 10 === 0) out.push({n: i + 1, p: (c + 1) / (i + 2)});
  });
  return out;
})()

card = (label, value, colour) => html`<div class="sim-readout">
  <div class="sim-readout-label">${label}</div>
  <div class="sim-readout-value" style="color:${colour}">${value}</div>
</div>`

html`<div class="sim-readouts">
  ${card("Observed difference", observed.toFixed(3) + " g", "#ef4444")}
  ${card("At least as extreme", count + " of " + nShuffles, "#f59e0b")}
  ${card("Running p-value", pRun.toFixed(4), "#38bdf8")}
  ${card("Exact p (all 12,870 splits)", exactP.toFixed(4), "#10b981")}
</div>`

// Bin edges sit between the values a difference can take, so no value lands on an edge.
edges = Array.from({length: 33}, (_, k) => -0.40125 + 0.025 * k)

Plot.plot({
  height: 300,
  marginLeft: 50,
  // Plot paints its own white ground otherwise, which the dark card fights.
  style: {background: "transparent", color: "#cbd5e1"},
  x: {domain: [-0.42, 0.42], label: "Treated − control (g) →"},
  y: {label: "↑ Shuffles", grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Less extreme", "At least as extreme", "Observed"],
          range: ["#38bdf8", "#f59e0b", "#ef4444"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(shown, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: d => d, thresholds: edges,
      fill: d => extreme(d) ? "At least as extreme" : "Less extreme"})),
    Plot.ruleX([observed, -observed], {stroke: () => "Observed", strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "5 3"}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})

Plot.plot({
  height: 200,
  marginLeft: 50,
  style: {background: "transparent", color: "#cbd5e1"},
  x: {label: "Shuffles drawn →", domain: [0, Math.max(nShuffles, 100)]},
  y: {label: "↑ Running p-value", domain: [0, 0.2], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([exactP], {stroke: "#10b981", strokeDasharray: "6 4"}),
    Plot.line(running, {x: "n", y: "p", stroke: "#38bdf8", strokeWidth: 2, clip: true}),
    Plot.text([{n: Math.max(nShuffles, 100), p: exactP}], {x: "n", y: "p", text: () => "exact", dy: -8, textAnchor: "end", fill: "#10b981"})
  ]
})
```

The shuffles come from a fixed seed, so every reader sees the same ones.
:::

With the means, the treated bushes are 0.220 g heavier. At 1,000 shuffles, 63 are at least as extreme, so $p = 64/1001 = 0.0639$; at 5,000, 307 are, so $p = 308/5001 = 0.0616$, against the exact 0.0615 (792 of the 12,870 splits). Welch's t-test on the same numbers gives 0.064, so here the two agree.

## Any statistic, exact or random

Nothing in the recipe needs the statistic to be a difference in means; it only has to be computed the same way on every shuffle. That is the main practical gain over the t-test. On the same data the exact p-value is 0.0615 for the difference in means, 0.0295 for the difference in 25% trimmed means (the mean of the middle half of each group), and 0.0140 for the difference in medians. The reason is one control bush at 2.12 g, heavier than every treated bush. The control mean moves with every gram of it; the median and the trimmed mean register only that it is the heaviest bush, not by how much.

That spread is also a warning. Three statistics, three p-values, and the one you report must be the one you chose before looking. Picking the smallest afterwards makes every one of them wrong, for the reasons in [What a p-value is not](p-values/what_a_p_value_is_not.ipynb). My own rule, not a tested one: if the measurements you collect often contain odd units, such as a bush with a damaged neighbour or a mislabelled crate, decide on medians or trimmed means in the analysis plan, not after the data arrive.

**Exact or Monte Carlo.** An exact test goes through every labelling; a Monte Carlo test draws a random sample of them. The count explodes quickly: $\binom{16}{8} = 12{,}870$, but $\binom{30}{15} = 155{,}117{,}520$. Beyond small groups, then, the test is Monte Carlo. My own rule: use 9,999 shuffles or more when the answer is near your threshold, because a Monte Carlo p-value carries sampling error from the shuffles, with standard error

$$\mathrm{SE}(p) \approx \sqrt{\frac{p(1 - p)}{m}}$$

where $p$ is the p-value and $m$ the number of shuffles. Near $p = 0.05$, 9,999 shuffles give $\sqrt{0.05 \times 0.95 / 9999} = 0.0022$. In the widget, medians at 5,000 shuffles read 0.0120 against the exact 0.0140, about 1.2 standard errors away, since $\sqrt{0.014 \times 0.986 / 5000} = 0.0017$.

In scipy, `permutation_test` does the shuffling for any statistic you pass it, and switches to the exact test when `n_resamples` is at least the number of distinct labellings. The cell below is the one to copy.

```python
# Copy this. One value per independent unit; with several berries per bush,
# average first: df.groupby("bush")["weight"].mean().
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

treated = np.array([1.76, 1.91, 1.84, 1.58, 1.98, 1.97, 1.67, 1.86])  # synthetic, the widget's data (g)
control = np.array([1.54, 1.40, 1.47, 2.12, 1.79, 1.75, 1.36, 1.38])


def diff_medians(x, y, axis):  # chosen before looking at the data
    return np.median(x, axis=axis) - np.median(y, axis=axis)


def welch_t(x, y, axis):  # use when the spreads may differ
    return stats.ttest_ind(x, y, equal_var=False, axis=axis).statistic


for name, stat in [("difference in medians", diff_medians), ("Welch t", welch_t)]:
    exact = stats.permutation_test((treated, control), stat, n_resamples=np.inf, vectorized=True)
    mc = stats.permutation_test((treated, control), stat, n_resamples=9999, vectorized=True,
                                rng=np.random.default_rng(1))
    print(f"{name} {exact.statistic:.3f}: exact p = {exact.pvalue:.4f}, "
          f"Monte Carlo p = {mc.pvalue:.4f} from {len(mc.null_distribution)} shuffles")

# Paired (both treatments on each field): pass the differences as one sample;
# permutation_type="samples" flips the sign of each, i.e. swaps labels within each pair.
d = np.random.default_rng(2).normal(0.15, 0.2, 10)  # synthetic treated - control, 10 fields
paired = stats.permutation_test((d,), lambda d, axis: d.mean(axis=axis), permutation_type="samples",
                                n_resamples=np.inf, vectorized=True)
print(f"paired: mean difference {paired.statistic:.3f} g, exact p = {paired.pvalue:.4f} "
      f"over {len(paired.null_distribution)} sign patterns")
```

```
difference in medians 0.345: exact p = 0.0140, Monte Carlo p = 0.0130 from 9999 shuffles
Welch t 2.062: exact p = 0.0615, Monte Carlo p = 0.0606 from 9999 shuffles
paired: mean difference 0.149 g, exact p = 0.0742 over 1024 sign patterns
```

The exact p-values match the widget, and with these equal-sized groups shuffling Welch's t gives the same exact p-value as the difference in means. scipy's two-sided p-value is twice the smaller one-sided one, not the absolute-difference share the widget uses; the two agree here because equal-sized groups give a symmetric null distribution.

Unlike [bootstrapping](bootstrapping/bootstrapping.ipynb), which resamples *with* replacement to estimate how much an estimate varies, a permutation test moves labels *without* replacement to test a null, and says nothing about effect size, so report the difference and its interval too.

## Shuffle what was randomised

The shuffle stands in for the randomisation, so it must move the same things the randomisation moved. If treatments were assigned to bushes, a shuffle moves whole bushes, with all their berries together. Shuffling individual berries pretends each berry was randomised on its own, and it inherits the pseudo-replication error from [the t-test module](t-test/the_t_test.ipynb). In the same setup, 5 bushes per treatment, 10 berries each, intraclass correlation 0.5 and no treatment effect, shuffling berries gives 43.5% false positives and shuffling whole bushes 4.4% (the simulation code is in the next section). A different test does not rescue a wrong unit.

Restricted designs need restricted shuffles. In a **blocked** design, where each block (a row, a field, a harvest day) received every treatment, labels are shuffled only within each block, because that is the only reassignment the design could have produced. In a **paired** design each pair is a block of two, so the only shuffle is swapping the two labels within a pair, which flips the sign of that pair's difference. With 10 pairs there are $2^{10} = 1024$ sign patterns, few enough to test exactly, as the paired line of the copy cell does. By the same logic (my inference, untested), consecutive days of a time series cannot be shuffled freely.

## What it assumes, and when it fails

If the spreads may differ, shuffle Welch's t, not the raw difference. The reason is the test's one condition: under the null, the labelled groups are exchangeable, which for two independent groups means they come from the same distribution. That null is stronger than "the means are equal". If the treatment leaves the mean alone but doubles the spread, the groups are not exchangeable, and a test of the difference in means is no longer guaranteed to hold its stated rate of false positives. Chung and Romano show that permutation tests comparing parameters such as means or medians need not keep their nominal false-positive rate, not even approximately in large samples, and give a procedure that stays exact when the distributions are identical and becomes valid in large samples when only the parameters are equal[^3].

The simulation below repeats the unequal-spread cases from [the t-test module](t-test/the_t_test.ipynb): no true difference in means, so the ideal false-positive rate is 5%. Each synthetic experiment is tested by shuffling, once with the raw difference in means as the statistic and once with Welch's t.

| Case: (n, SD) vs (n, SD) | Raw difference | Welch's t |
|---|---|---|
| (10, 1) vs (10, 1) | 4.9% | 4.5% |
| (6, 3) vs (24, 1) | 26.8% | 7.6% |
| (24, 3) vs (6, 1) | 0.4% | 3.5% |

: False-positive rate of a permutation test, 2,000 synthetic experiments per row, 999 shuffles each. {.striped}

With equal spreads both statistics hold 5%. With a small noisy group, shuffling the raw difference gives 26.8% false positives. Student's t-test gave 26.8% on the same case in the t-test module; those are separate simulations with different seeds and numbers of experiments, so the exact match is a coincidence, but the size of the failure is the same. My own explanation, not tested: the shuffles mix the two spreads just as Student's pooled variance does. Using Welch's t as the statistic brings it to 7.6%, better but not 5% with only 6 units in the small group; Welch's t-test with its own t distribution gave 5.3% on that case in the t-test module. So shuffling does not remove the unequal-variance problem; the statistic has to handle it. My own rule: if you do not know whether the spreads are equal, use Welch's t as the statistic. It costs little: it held 4.5% in the equal-spread row, and in the t-test module Welch's t-test gave up under one percentage point of power to Student's when spreads were equal (55.8% against 56.3%).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Simulation code

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(1935)
REPS, M = 2000, 999  # synthetic experiments; random shuffles per experiment


def perm_p(y, n1, stat):  # Monte Carlo two-sided p-value, labels shuffled across all of y
    obs = stat(y[:n1], y[n1:])
    shuf = rng.permuted(np.tile(y, (M, 1)), axis=1)
    null = stat(shuf[:, :n1], shuf[:, n1:])
    return (np.sum(np.abs(null) >= abs(obs) - 1e-12) + 1) / (M + 1)


diff = lambda a, b: a.mean(-1) - b.mean(-1)
welch_t = lambda a, b: stats.ttest_ind(a, b, axis=-1, equal_var=False).statistic

# Unequal spreads, equal true means: does shuffling the raw difference hold 5%?
for n1, sd1, n2, sd2 in [(10, 1, 10, 1), (6, 3, 24, 1), (24, 3, 6, 1)]:
    p = np.array([[perm_p(y, n1, s) for s in (diff, welch_t)]
                  for y in (np.r_[rng.normal(0, sd1, n1), rng.normal(0, sd2, n2)] for _ in range(REPS))])
    print(f"({n1}, SD {sd1}) vs ({n2}, SD {sd2}): false positives, raw difference {np.mean(p[:, 0] < 0.05):.3f}, "
          f"Welch t as the statistic {np.mean(p[:, 1] < 0.05):.3f}")

# 5 bushes per treatment, 10 berries each, ICC 0.5, no treatment effect: shuffle berries or bushes?
fp = np.zeros(2)
for _ in range(REPS):
    berries = (rng.normal(0, 0.3, (10, 1)) + rng.normal(0, 0.3, (10, 10)))  # rows are bushes, first 5 treated
    fp += [perm_p(berries.ravel(), 50, diff) < 0.05, perm_p(berries.mean(1), 5, diff) < 0.05]
print(f"false positives: shuffling berries {fp[0] / REPS:.3f}, shuffling whole bushes {fp[1] / REPS:.3f}")
```

```
(10, SD 1) vs (10, SD 1): false positives, raw difference 0.049, Welch t as the statistic 0.045
(6, SD 3) vs (24, SD 1): false positives, raw difference 0.268, Welch t as the statistic 0.076
(24, SD 3) vs (6, SD 1): false positives, raw difference 0.004, Welch t as the statistic 0.035
false positives: shuffling berries 0.435, shuffling whole bushes 0.044
```

Shuffling whole bushes is done here by shuffling bush means, which is the same thing when every bush has the same number of berries. The bush-level test with 10 bushes could be exact, with $\binom{10}{5} = 252$ splits; the Monte Carlo version is used for both so that only the unit differs.
:::

## Key takeaways

- Write down the statistic, and whether the test is one- or two-sided, before the data arrive; if you try others afterwards, report all of them.
- Shuffle the units that were randomised, within the blocks or pairs the design used. If you cannot say what the randomisation was, the permutation test has nothing to imitate.
- Report $p = (b + 1)/(m + 1)$, never $b/m$, and use enough shuffles that the Monte Carlo error is small next to the distance from your threshold.
- When spreads may differ between groups, use Welch's t as the shuffled statistic, or Welch's t-test itself; shuffling a raw difference does not fix unequal variances.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What this means for you

A permutation test lets you test the statistic you actually care about, a median, a trimmed mean, a difference in the share of fruit above a grade, without a formula for its standard error. It is only as good as the shuffle: it is exact when the shuffle copies the randomisation and the groups would share a distribution under the null, and Chung and Romano show it can fail when they only share a mean[^3]. My own inference: for a routine two-group comparison of independent units, run Welch's t-test and a permutation test of your pre-chosen statistic; if they disagree, look at the data before trusting either.
:::

## References

[^1]: Phipson, B. & Smyth, G. K. Permutation P-values should never be zero: calculating exact P-values when permutations are randomly drawn. *Stat. Appl. Genet. Mol. Biol.* **9**(1) (2010). https://doi.org/10.2202/1544-6115.1585
[^2]: Ernst, M. D. Permutation methods: a basis for exact inference. *Stat. Sci.* **19**, 676–685 (2004). https://doi.org/10.1214/088342304000000396
[^3]: Chung, E. & Romano, J. P. Exact and asymptotically robust permutation tests. *Ann. Stat.* **41**, 484–507 (2013). https://doi.org/10.1214/13-AOS1090
